newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait MP stable after attempt on his life.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait MP stable after attempt on his life.

text.p: A leading Kuwaiti opposition parliamentarian was reported to be in stable condition in hospital on Saturday after he was shot in an assassination attempt.

The government said Abdullah al-Naibari and his wife underwent successful operations after gunmen ambushed their car on Friday and opened fire as they drove back to Kuwait City from a beach near the southern border with Saudi Arabia.

A senior official told Reuters that the authorities were questioning witnesses who said two cars were involved in the attack on Naibari, 61, a leading government critic who also opposed some Islamist bills in parliament.
Naibari was hit in the jaw and shoulder by bullets while his wife suffered a superficial bullet wound near her left shoulder.
The government condemned the shooting and promised to conduct an intensive inquiry to secure the arrest of the gunmen.
Members of Kuwait's ruling al-Sabah family, ministers, senior officials and members of parliament gathered at the Adan Hospital, south of Kuwait City, where the couple were being treated.
Several MPs, of various affiliations, said the attack was politically motivated by what they called the enemies of democracy in the small Gulf Arab state.
Kuwait, which controls about 10 percent of the world's proven oil reserves, is the only one of the six conservative Sunni Moslem-ruled Gulf Arab states with an elected parliament.
Some political sources suggested that Naibari might have created many enemies by asking frequent questions in parliament about arms deals and what they called the "stealing of public funds."

Fellow liberal MP Sami al-Munayes said: "It is a battle between right and wrong and defending the people's rights." He urged the government "to strike with an iron fist, with deeds and not words," at all forms of corruption.
Parliamentary speaker Ahmad al-Saadoun told journalists at the hospital that "corrupt elements" were behind the shooting.

Leading Islamist MP Adnan Abdel-Samad, a Shi'ite, said some Kuwaitis whose intrests were harmed by parliament's relentless questioning about the country's vast oil wealth were behind the attack. He did not name them.
Naibari, a pro-democracy veteran, played a key role in parliamentary efforts since 1992 to combat what the opposition described as graft and mismanagement of state funds.
Foreign Minister Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Sabah, the acting prime minister, said the attack was directed "against the Kuwaiti people and Kuwait" and was meant to trigger "strife".

Political killings are rare in Gulf Arab states but former MP Hamad al-Jouan was crippled in an attempt on his life in 1991, weeks after Kuwait was freed from a seven-month Iraqi occupation by U.S.-led forces in the Gulf War.
Jouan and Naibari were members of parliament when it was dissolved in 1986 and both were leading members of a campaign for its restoration, which was achieved in 1992.
